entry: German-American entrepreneur and venture capitalist. He co-founded [[PayPal]] in 1998 and was its chief executive officer until its sale to [[EBay|eBay]] in 2002 for $1.5 billion. He launched the data analysis company Palantir Technologies in 2003, has chaired it since, and founded the venture firm Founders Fund in 2005. In August 2004 he became the first outside investor in [[Facebook]], acquiring a 10.2% stake for $500,000. Commentators have portrayed his political views as conservative libertarian and, in some accounts, democracy-skeptic authoritarian.

Tsar of Russia (1682–1721) and first emperor of Russia (1721–25). He reigned jointly with his brother, Ivan V, until Ivan's death in 1696. Much of his reign was consumed by wars against the Ottoman and Swedish empires. After victory in the [[Great Northern War]], Russia annexed a significant part of the eastern Baltic coastline and was officially raised from a tsardom to an empire. He introduced the [[Julian calendar]] in December 1699 and the first Russian newspaper in 1703. On the shores of the [[Neva|Neva River]] he founded [[Saint Petersburg]], which replaced [[Moscow]] as the capital in 1712 and retained that status until 1918. His administrative reforms, including the Governing Senate (1711), the Collegium (1717) and the Table of Ranks (1722), had a lasting impact. He is primarily credited with modernizing the country, though his reforms were largely imposed from above.

Ancient city and archaeological site in southern [[Jordan]], carved into [[Sandstone|sandstone]] cliffs. Its rock-cut architecture and water conduit systems made it famous, and it is called the "Rose City" for the color of its stone. Settled by the Nabataeans, a nomadic Arab people, in the 4th century BC, it became the capital of the Nabataean Kingdom and a trading hub on the incense routes. Its Al-Khazneh structure, possibly the mausoleum of Nabataean king Aretas IV, dates from the 1st century AD, when the population peaked at an estimated 20,000. The Romans annexed Nabataea in AD 106 and renamed it Arabia Petraea. An earthquake in 363 destroyed many structures, and by the early Islamic era the city was largely abandoned. The Swiss traveler Johann Ludwig Burckhardt rediscovered it in 1812. It receives close to a million visitors a year. [[UNESCO]] designated it a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1985.

Italian scholar and poet, one of the earliest Renaissance [[Humanism|humanists]]. His rediscovery of [[Cicero]]'s letters is often credited with initiating the 14th-century Italian Renaissance and the founding of Renaissance humanism. In 1345 he discovered a collection of Cicero's letters not previously known to exist, *Epistulae ad Atticum*, in the chapter library of Verona Cathedral. His Latin epic *Africa*, about the Roman general [[Scipio Africanus]], made him a European celebrity, and on April 8, 1341, he was crowned poet laureate on Rome's Capitoline Hill. His *Canzoniere*, a sequence of 366 poems largely inspired by his unrequited love for Laura, established the Petrarchan [[Sonnet|sonnet]] form that influenced European literature for centuries. In the 16th century, Pietro Bembo based the model for modern Italian on Petrarch's works. He is also credited with being the first to develop the concept of the "Dark Ages".

Chemical product obtained from [[Petroleum|petroleum]] by refining. Some petrochemicals are also obtained from other fossil fuels, such as coal or natural gas, or from renewable sources such as maize, palm fruit or sugar cane. The two most common classes are olefins, including [[Ethylene|ethylene]] and propylene, and aromatics, including [[Benzene|benzene]], toluene and xylene isomers. Olefins and aromatics are building blocks for solvents, [[Detergent|detergents]], adhesives, [[Plastic|plastics]], resins, fibers, elastomers, lubricants and gels. Global ethylene production was 190 million tonnes and propylene 120 million tonnes in 2019, and aromatics production was approximately 70 million tonnes. The largest petrochemical industries are in the United States and Western Europe, but major growth in production capacity is in the Middle East and Asia.

Quasi-solid mixture of [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]], also called petrolatum, used as a topical ointment. Workers on early U.S. oil rigs noticed a paraffin-like substance in 1859 and used it on cuts and burns. Robert Chesebrough opened his first factory in [[Brooklyn]] in 1870 under the name Vaseline, which has been the dominant brand since then. He patented the refining process in 1872 (U.S. patent 127,568). Petroleum jelly is widely recognized as a skin protectant and is common in [[Cosmetics|cosmetic]] skin care, where it is often loosely called mineral oil.

Branch of [[Geology|geology]] that studies rocks, their [[Mineralogy|mineralogy]], composition, texture and structure, and the conditions under which they form. Petrology has three subdivisions: igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary petrology. Igneous and metamorphic petrology are commonly taught together because both make heavy use of chemistry, chemical methods and phase diagrams, while sedimentary petrology is commonly taught with [[Stratigraphy]] because it deals with the processes that form sedimentary rock. Igneous petrology examines rocks such as [[Granite|granite]] and basalt, which crystallized from [[Magma|magma]]. Sedimentary petrology examines rocks such as sandstone, shale and limestone, made of particles from other rocks or of biological or chemical deposits. Metamorphic petrology examines rocks such as [[Marble|marble]], slate, gneiss and schist, which have changed through pressure, temperature or both.

French automobile brand owned by Stellantis. The Peugeot family began manufacturing in 1810 with a steel foundry that made saws, and Automobiles Peugeot was created in 1896, making it the oldest car company in the world. Armand Peugeot built the company's first vehicle, a steam-powered tricycle. Peugeot vehicles have received six European Car of the Year awards. In motorsport, the brand won the Indianapolis 500 in 1913, 1916 and 1919, and Peugeot Sport has won the World Rally Championship five times and the [[24 Hours of Le Mans]] three times.

Malleable metal [[Alloy|alloy]] traditionally of [[Tin|tin]] and as much as 40% [[Lead|lead]]. Modern pewter replaces lead with [[Antimony|antimony]] (approximately 5–10%), copper (2%), bismuth and sometimes silver, and it melts at around 170–230 °C. The earliest known piece was found in an Egyptian tomb, dated to c. 1450 BC. Pewter was a leading material for plates, cups and bowls in Europe from the Middle Ages until the wide adoption of [[Porcelain|porcelain]] and glass. Today it is used mainly for decorative objects, collectible statuettes, replica coins and jewelry.

American former professional football quarterback in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He spent 14 seasons with the [[Indianapolis]] Colts, winning [[Super Bowl]] XLI, and four with the [[Denver]] Broncos, winning Super Bowl 50. Selected first overall in the 1998 NFL draft, he holds many league records, including most MVP awards. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2021. He is the older brother of former NFL quarterback Eli Manning.

Current and most recent of the four eons of the [[Geologic time scale|geologic time scale]], spanning from 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago to the present. The name, from Greek words meaning "visible" and "life," was coined in 1930 by the American geologist George Halcott Chadwick. It is the eon in which abundant animal and plant life proliferated, diversified and colonized various niches, beginning with the [[Cambrian]] period, when animals first developed hard shells that are preserved in the fossil record. The Phanerozoic is divided into the [[Paleozoic]], [[Mesozoic]] and [[Cenozoic]] eras, which together contain 12 periods. Plate tectonics assembled the continents into [[Pangaea]], the most recent supercontinent, before it fragmented. The Cenozoic began with the extinction of all non-avian dinosaurs, and humans appeared during its most recent part. The earlier time is called the [[Precambrian]].

Title of the rulers of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]]. The word derives from an Egyptian compound meaning "great house," originally referring to the royal palace. The earliest confirmed use of the title for a ruler is in a letter to [[Akhenaten]] of the Eighteenth Dynasty, and it was later attributed to all earlier kings. Scholars use it for all rulers from the First Dynasty (c. 3150 BC) until Egypt was annexed by the [[Roman Republic]] in 30 BC. The king acted as an intermediary between the deities and the people, owned all the land, enacted laws, collected taxes and commanded the military. He was responsible for maintaining *Maat*, or cosmic order, and chose the sites of new temples. Early kings wore the Red Crown of Lower Egypt or the White Crown of Upper Egypt; after unification they wore the Pschent, a combination of both.

Healthcare professional with expertise in [[Medication|medications]], also called a chemist in Commonwealth English (excluding Canada). Pharmacists undergo university or graduate-level education in drug mechanisms, side effects, interactions and monitoring, and they dispense medications safely to the public. Pharmacists often serve as primary care providers in their communities, offering health screenings and immunizations. Countries require a Bachelor of Pharmacy, Master of Pharmacy or Doctor of Pharmacy degree, depending on the country. The most common positions are community pharmacist, in retail settings, and hospital pharmacist, who counsels patients on the proper use and adverse effects of prescribed drugs. In some jurisdictions pharmacists may prescribe or administer certain medications, and others work in industry, research, academia and government. Historically, pharmacists checked and distributed drugs to doctors; today they advise patients and prescribers on dosages, interactions and side effects.

Branch of [[Pharmacology|pharmacology]] that studies how the body affects a substance after administration, often abbreviated PK. The substances include pharmaceutical drugs, [[Pesticide|pesticides]], food additives and [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]]. PK traces the fate of a chemical from administration until it is completely eliminated, using mathematical models of the relationship between drug plasma concentration and time. Pharmacokinetics describes what the organism does to a drug, whereas pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body. The processes are summarized as ADME: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, with liberation sometimes added as a first step. Metabolism, mainly in the [[Liver|liver]], breaks the drug down through enzymes such as cytochrome P450. With regular dosing, steady state is generally reached after 3 to 5 times the drug's half-life.

Science of drugs and medications, including their origin, composition and interaction with biological systems. Its two main areas are pharmacodynamics, which studies the effects of a drug on biological systems, and [[Pharmacokinetics|pharmacokinetics]], which studies the effects of biological systems on a drug. Pharmacodynamics examines how chemicals bind to biological receptors, and pharmacokinetics tracks their liberation, absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. The field includes [[Toxicology|toxicology]], therapy and drug design. Pharmacology is not synonymous with [[Pharmacy|pharmacy]], which applies its principles in clinical care. The origins of clinical pharmacology lie in the Middle Ages, with [[Avicenna]]'s *The Canon of Medicine*, and early work focused on herbalism and plant extracts. Modern pharmacology emerged in the late 19th century.

Science and practice of dispensing, preparing, monitoring and consulting about [[Medication|medications]], aiming for their safe, effective and affordable use. The practice is clinically oriented, with most drugs manufactured by pharmaceutical industries. Pharmacy practice is classified as community or institutional. Clinical pharmacy, the direct care of patients, is mainly practiced in hospitals, long-term care facilities, hospices, ambulatory clinics and psychiatric hospitals. [[Pharmacist|Pharmacists]] are considered the experts on drug therapy. In some jurisdictions, such as Colorado, Canada and Australia, they have more liberty to prescribe or adapt prescriptions. In the United States and Canada, drugstores also sell [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]], office supplies, [[Toy|toys]] and [[Magazine|magazines]]. Pharmacy is distinct from [[Pharmacology|pharmacology]], a biomedical science, although the two are closely related and often confused.

American musician, singer, songwriter, record producer and fashion designer. He first became known as one half of the production duo the Neptunes, formed with Chad Hugo in 1992, whose productions include four songs that peaked atop the Billboard Hot 100. He also served as lead vocalist of the rock and [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] band N.E.R.D. His 2013 single "Happy" also reached number one and was nominated for an Academy Award. He has won 13 Grammy Awards, and he has been men's creative director of Louis Vuitton since 2023.

Chart used to show the conditions of pressure, temperature and other variables under which thermodynamically distinct [[Phase (matter)|phases]] occur and coexist at equilibrium. Lines on the diagram, called phase boundaries, mark conditions under which phases coexist, and phase transitions occur along them. Where lines intersect, a [[Triple point]] marks conditions at which three phases coexist; for water this is 273.16 K and a partial vapor pressure of 611.657 Pa. The liquid–gas boundary ends at the [[Critical point (thermodynamics)|critical point]], beyond which the liquid and gaseous phases become indistinguishable. Water's critical point is at Tc = 647.096 K (373.946 °C), pc = 22.064 MPa (217.75 atm). The solidus is the temperature below which a substance is stable as a solid, and the liquidus is the temperature above which it is stable as a liquid. Phase diagrams are essential in metallurgy and materials science, where they guide the design of alloys.

Region of a material that is chemically uniform, physically distinct and often mechanically separable. In a glass jar holding ice and water, the ice, the water and the humid air above them are each a separate phase, and the glass is a fourth. The term is sometimes used as a synonym for [[State of matter|state of matter]], but several immiscible phases can exist within one state, as with oil and water both in the liquid state. Distinct phases may be gas, liquid, solid, [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] or Bose–Einstein condensate, and useful mesophases lie between solid and liquid. As many as eight immiscible liquid phases have been observed. Phases do not always separate spontaneously: [[Emulsion|emulsions]] and [[Colloid|colloids]] are immiscible combinations that stay mixed.

Physical process of transition between one state of a medium and another. The term commonly refers to changes among the basic states of matter: solid, liquid and gas, and in rare cases plasma. During a transition, certain properties of the medium change as external conditions such as temperature or pressure change, often abruptly. A liquid may become a gas on heating to its [[Boiling point|boiling point]], with an abrupt change in volume. The conditions at which the transformation occurs define the transition point. Below the boiling point the liquid is the more stable state, whereas above it the gas is. Changes can also occur within a single state, such as when a solid changes crystal structure; this is called [[Allotropy|allotropy]] in elements and polymorphism in compounds. The best-known magnetic transition is the change between ferromagnetic and paramagnetic phases at the Curie point.

Common bean, *Phaseolus vulgaris*, a herbaceous annual [[Legume|legume]] of the family Fabaceae. Bush varieties form erect plants 20–60 centimeters tall, while pole varieties form vines 2–3 meters long. The plant is native to the [[Americas]], where it was domesticated in Mexico, Central America and the southern [[Andes]] region some 8,000 years ago. It is the most consumed bean species in the world; in 2022, 28 million tonnes of dry common beans were produced worldwide, led by India with 23% of the total. Raw dry beans contain the toxic protein phytohaemagglutinin, which is deactivated by [[Boiling|boiling]] the beans for 30 minutes. The unripe green pods are also eaten, and the leaves are occasionally used as a vegetable.

Order of [[Insect|insects]] known as stick insects, stick bugs or walkingsticks, including the leaf insects. Members are found on all continents except Antarctica and are most abundant in the tropics and subtropics. They are herbivorous and nocturnal, and their [[Camouflage|camouflage]] makes them difficult for predators to detect. Many species have secondary defenses such as startle displays, spines or toxic secretions. The genera Phryganistria, Ctenomorpha and Phobaeticus include the world's longest insects; females of an undescribed Phryganistria species, informally known as "chinensis," can reach 64 centimeters (25 inches) in total length. Many phasmids are parthenogenetic, and their life cycle has three stages: egg, [[Nymph (biology)|nymph]] and adult.

Dissociative anesthetic, mainly used recreationally for its mind-altering effects, also known as PCP or angel dust. It works primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist. PCP may cause [[Hallucination|hallucinations]], distorted perceptions and psychotic behavior, and it is typically smoked, though it may be swallowed, snorted or injected. Adverse effects include paranoia, [[Addiction|addiction]] and an increased risk of [[Suicide|suicide]], as well as seizures and [[Coma|coma]] in cases of overdose. Flashbacks may occur after use stops. As of 2022, about 0.7% of 12th-grade students in the United States reported using PCP in the prior year.

Aromatic organic compound, C₆H₅OH, also called carbolic acid. Phenol is a white crystalline solid that is volatile and can catch fire. Its molecule consists of a phenyl group bonded to a hydroxy group. It is mildly acidic, can cause chemical burns and is acutely toxic. Phenol was first extracted from [[Coal|coal]] tar, but it is now produced on a large scale, about 7 million tonnes a year, from petroleum-derived feedstocks. It is primarily used to make plastics and related materials, including [[Polycarbonate|polycarbonates]], [[Epoxy|epoxies]], [[Bakelite]] and [[Nylon|nylon]]. It is also a precursor to [[Explosive|explosives]] such as picric acid, to [[Detergent|detergents]], to phenoxy herbicides and to numerous pharmaceutical drugs.

Philosophical method and movement of the early 20th century, concerned with the structures of conscious experience as they appear. The tradition was inaugurated by [[Edmund Husserl|Edmund Husserl]], whose transcendental phenomenology sought universal logical structures in subjective experience. Phenomenology seeks to describe the universal features of consciousness while avoiding assumptions about the external world. Its central concept is intentionality, the idea that consciousness is always directed toward an object. The term first appeared in direct connection with Husserl's philosophy in a 1907 article in *The Philosophical Review*. [[Martin Heidegger|Martin Heidegger]] argued that truths are contextually situated and depend on historical and cultural context, and other branches include hermeneutic, genetic and embodied phenomenology. The approach has been applied to qualitative research in psychology, the social sciences, the humanities and cognitive science.
